prompt: What did curl print while shipquote was being restarted?

choices.text: 503, the status of a service that is starting
choices.why: Nothing answered to send a status.

choices.text: 000, because the connection was refused
choices.why: Right. No process held the port.

choices.text: 200, the old process answered until the new one took over
choices.why: The old one was stopped first.

choices.text: 500, from the new release's start-up error
choices.why: There was no error; there was no process.

prompt: How many health checks in a row got no answer during the restart?
When is recreate the right strategy, by the lesson?

choices.text: When the service has many instances
choices.why: Many instances are what rolling updates use.

choices.text: When the release changes only the user interface
choices.why: A UI change is what two versions handle well.

choices.text: When two versions must never overlap
choices.why: Right. It is the one strategy where they never overlap.

choices.text: When the deploy happens during business hours
choices.why: That is when its gap hurts most.

prompt: What adds to the gap of a recreate deploy? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The old process shutting down
choices.why: Right. The port is busy until it lets go.

choices.text: The interpreter starting and importing the program
choices.why: Right. Every start pays it.

choices.text: Work done before listening, like warming a cache
choices.why: Right. The port opens only after it.

choices.text: The number of tests in the suite
choices.why: Tests run before the deploy, not inside it.

prompt: What does a rolling update trade for having no gap in service?

choices.text: Two versions serve customers during the rollout
choices.why: Right. The middle steps run both.

choices.text: A second complete copy of production, running all the time
choices.why: That is blue-green's price.

choices.text: Code paths for both behaviours
choices.why: That is a feature flag's price.

choices.text: A longer test suite
choices.why: The suite is unchanged.

prompt: Four instances. Match each setting to what it does during the rollout.

pairs.right: Serves with three instances, no extra machine
Starts a fifth instance so capacity never drops

right_distractors: Stops all four, then starts all four

prompt: Release 2 writes data that release 1 cannot read. What goes wrong in a rolling update?

choices.text: The load balancer refuses the new instances
choices.why: It has no idea what the data looks like.

choices.text: Some later requests land on old instances
choices.why: Right. It meets data it cannot read.

choices.text: The rollout stops by itself at the first error
choices.why: Nothing in the strategy compares the versions.

choices.text: The new instances fail their health check
choices.why: Health checks do not read stored data.

prompt: How does ops/router.py decide which side serves a request?

choices.text: It alternates, one request each
choices.why: There is no counter in it.

choices.text: It picks the side that answered faster last time
choices.why: It measures nothing.

choices.text: A hash of X-Request-Id
choices.why: Right. The same id lands on the same side.

choices.text: The customer's CEP
choices.why: The router never reads the query.

prompt: During the switch to green, how many of the 2000 requests went unanswered?
The smoke test passed on green, and green then failed one order in twenty. Why did the smoke test miss it?

choices.text: It ran against blue by mistake
choices.why: It ran against port 8302, green.

choices.text: It only checks /health and the version
choices.why: Right. It asked whether 1.6.0 was running, and it was.

choices.text: The bug appears only under load
choices.why: One request to Alagoas reproduces it.

choices.text: Smoke tests skip the quote endpoint by rule
choices.why: No such rule; this one just does not ask.

prompt: In blue-green, the side not serving customers keeps ___ , so going back needs no deploy.
How long did switching back to blue take?

choices.text: About a second, the length of a restart
choices.why: Nothing was restarted.

choices.text: Three milliseconds
choices.why: Right. One edit to a file; blue never stopped.

choices.text: As long as building 1.5.0 again
choices.why: The 1.5.0 build already existed and was running.

choices.text: Five seconds, the router's timeout
choices.why: The timeout plays no part in a switch.

prompt: Green's log held 77 identical lines: error: ___ : 57.
Which are costs of blue-green, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A second production running
choices.why: Right. At least during each release.

choices.text: Every customer moves in one step
choices.why: Right. A bug reaches all of them until the flip back.

choices.text: Sessions kept in a process's memory are lost
choices.why: Right. Keep them in a store both sides read.

choices.text: Going back requires a rebuild
choices.why: Going back is the fast part.

prompt: Blue and green share one database. What must the release on green respect while switching back stays possible?

choices.text: It must not read the database until blue is gone
choices.why: It serves customers; it has to read.

choices.text: Blue must still work with the data green writes
choices.why: Right. The rolling update's rule applies here too.

choices.text: It needs its own copy of production's data
choices.why: Copying at every release is what the lesson calls impractical.

choices.text: It must run the same version of Python as blue
choices.why: Versions are not the point here.

prompt: At 10%, how many of green's 102 requests failed?
The same 1.6.0 failed 77 requests under blue-green and 2 as a canary. What made the difference?

choices.text: The canary run had fewer orders to Alagoas in its mix
choices.why: The mix was the same twenty orders.

choices.text: Green got one request in ten
choices.why: Right. A canary limits how far the bug reaches.

choices.text: The router retried green's errors on blue
choices.why: The router does not retry.

choices.text: 1.6.0 had been fixed in between
choices.why: The fix came in 1.6.1.

prompt: Order the steps of a canary rollout.
items: Deploy the new version beside the old
Send it a small share of traffic
Compare it with the old version
Widen the share, or send it back to 0
trap: Widening before comparing is the slip: the share grows on no evidence.

prompt: Why are a canary's first steps the smallest?

choices.text: Nothing is known yet; few are put at risk
choices.why: Right. Trust is earned step by step.

choices.text: The router cannot send more than 5% at first
choices.why: The router takes any weight.

choices.text: Small shares produce more precise measurements
choices.why: Small shares produce less evidence.

choices.text: To save the cost of green's machine
choices.why: Green runs whatever the share.

prompt: A rule says: stop the canary if its error rate is above 3%. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: 3% is too strict for any real service
choices.why: The number is not the problem.

choices.text: Error rates cannot be measured separately for each version
choices.why: The router's header does exactly that.

choices.text: It should count errors, not rates
choices.why: Counts depend on traffic; rates compare better.

choices.text: It ignores the baseline measured at the same time
choices.why: Right. It passes green's 2% and stops a fine release on a bad day.

prompt: Match each problem to the measurement that shows it first.

pairs.left: one request in a hundred takes five seconds
every answer is a 200 with a wrong price

prompt: The lab's router picks a side per request id. What does a real canary usually pick by, and why?

choices.text: By server load, to keep both sides equally busy
choices.why: That is load balancing, not a canary.

choices.text: By customer, one version each
choices.why: Right. Their experience is consistent and measurable.

choices.text: By region, so a bug is limited to one city
choices.why: A region-only canary measures one region.

choices.text: By time of day, sending night traffic to the canary
choices.why: Night traffic is a different mix.

prompt: Green fails 5% of requests. To have a 95% chance of seeing at least one error, how many requests must it answer?
hint: Find the smallest n with 0.95 to the power n below 0.05.

prompt: Green answered 8 requests without an error. What does that tell you about 1.6.0?

choices.text: That the bug is gone
choices.why: The same 1.6.0 failed in the next run.

choices.text: That its error rate is under 1%
choices.why: Eight requests cannot measure 1%.

choices.text: Nothing; a 5% bug passes 8 requests 66% of the time
choices.why: Right. 0.95 to the 8th is 66%.

choices.text: That the router is sending it the wrong orders from the mix
choices.why: The orders are the usual mix.

prompt: Why does ops/canary.py wait for 50 answers rather than for ten minutes?

choices.text: Ten minutes is longer than any canary should take
choices.why: Duration is not the concern.

choices.text: A clock holds less evidence at 3 a.m.
choices.why: Right. Evidence is a count of requests.

choices.text: A Python script cannot measure time
choices.why: It can.

choices.text: Fifty is the number of orders in the lab's fixed mix of requests
choices.why: The mix has twenty.

prompt: 1.6.1 took all the traffic with no flags file. What did customers see?

choices.text: A quote just like 1.5.0's, without days
choices.why: Right. The feature was deployed and off.

choices.text: An error, because the flags file was missing
choices.why: A missing file means no flags.

choices.text: The delivery estimate for every customer
choices.why: Nobody was in the flag.

choices.text: The estimate for 10% of customers
choices.why: The 10% came later, with the file.

prompt: Putting code in production with its feature switched off is called a dark ___ .
What does separating deploy from release make possible? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Deploying at any hour, since customers see no change
choices.why: Right. The risky moment moves to the flag.

choices.text: Merging an unfinished feature every day, switched off
choices.why: Right. No long-lived branch.

choices.text: Withdrawing a feature without a rollback
choices.why: Right. Turn the flag off.

choices.text: Skipping the tests for code behind a flag
choices.why: Code behind a flag still runs in production.

prompt: At 10%, how many of the thousand customers got the delivery estimate?
c3 had the estimate at 10%. Why does c3 still have it at 50%?

choices.text: The flag remembers who has seen the feature
choices.why: It stores nothing.

choices.text: c3 was added to an allow list
choices.why: There is no list.

choices.text: Its bucket was below 10, and so it is below 50 as well
choices.why: Right. Widening only adds buckets.

choices.text: The router keeps c3 on green
choices.why: Every customer is on green by then.

prompt: Why does flags.enabled hash the flag's name together with the customer's id?

choices.text: To make the bucket harder to guess
choices.why: Secrecy is not the point.

choices.text: Because sha256 needs at least two inputs
choices.why: It takes any bytes.

choices.text: So that a renamed flag keeps the same customers as before
choices.why: Renaming would change the buckets.

choices.text: So two flags at 10% pick different customers
choices.why: Right. Otherwise one tenth would test everything.

prompt: Match each flag to its kind.

pairs.left: delivery_estimate, until it is on for all
turn off the carrier call under pressure
the feature of a paid plan

prompt: With ten on-or-off flags, how many combinations can the program run in?
A release flag has been at 100% for a month. What should happen?

choices.text: Keep it, in case the feature has to be withdrawn
choices.why: That is a kill switch's job, and a test.

choices.text: Remove it and delete the losing path
choices.why: Right. A flag at 100% is a dead branch.

choices.text: Turn it into an experiment flag
choices.why: There is nothing left to compare.

choices.text: Move it to the configuration file of each environment
choices.why: It would still be two paths in the code.

prompt: Match each strategy to its way back.
A service takes a hundred requests a day and must be undone in seconds. Which fits, by the lesson?

choices.text: A canary at 1%
choices.why: It would see one request a day.

choices.text: Recreate, at night
choices.why: Undoing it is another deploy.

choices.text: Blue-green, with flags for its features
choices.why: Right. Fast way back, no need for traffic to judge.

choices.text: A rolling update across its single instance
choices.why: With one instance it is a recreate.

prompt: Which strategy limited 1.6.0's bug to the fewest failed requests in this lesson?

choices.text: Recreate
choices.why: 1.6.0 was never deployed by recreate here.

choices.text: Blue-green
choices.why: 77 failed before the flip back.

choices.text: The canary at 10%
choices.why: Right. Two failed of a thousand.

choices.text: The feature flag

prompt: Order this lesson's events as they happened.
items: Green gets 1.6.1 with the estimate off

prompt: Every strategy here limits a bug that got past the tests. What does none of them do?

choices.text: Reduce how many customers a bug reaches
choices.why: Canaries and flags do exactly that.

choices.text: Shorten how long a bug stays
choices.why: Blue-green brought it back in milliseconds.

choices.text: Stand in for the earlier tests
choices.why: Right. They limit damage; they do not find bugs early.

choices.text: Run two versions at once
choices.why: Most of them do.
